2.text: A necklace to which is attached a walrus-head carved in ivory is repre-

3.text: sented in the chapter on clothing.¹ Another amulet of this kind is shown in

4.text: Fig. 243, a. It consists of a double-headed dog carved in ivory and made like

5.text: a small toggle. The image and a single bead are tied to the back of the

6.text: leather belt.² This is considered an especially suitable place for wearing

7.text: amulets. The ermine-skin amulet which is sometimes attached to the neck-

8.text: lace is often fastened to the back of the belt instead.³ Fig. 243, b, is a

9.text: similar amulet worn on the belt of a Chukchee. It is made of wood, and

10.text: represents a canoe with paddle. The shape is quite similar to a wooden

11.text: button of the Baffin-Land Eskimo described by Boas.⁴

12.text: Human or animal “faces” are frequently carved on the handles of snow-

13.text: beaters for the purpose of giving protection to their owners. The snow-

14.text: beaters are then called “having a face” (g̣eluˊᵋlqᴀʟ̣in), Fig. 243, c.⁵

16.text: snow-beater with a carved face is especially important for a man who has to

17.text: live alone in the wilderness, like a herdsman or a hunter.

18.text: Fig. 244 is a “guardian” in the shape of a dog, but with a human face

19.text: on the front of the muzzle. It is covered with a coat made of skin. Com-

20.text: binations of animal figures with additional human faces are often met with on

21.text: the carvings of the American Eskimo.⁶
